subject: atomic bomb test
title: What If the First Atomic Bomb Had Set the Sky on Fire? Physicists Checked

scenes.text: What if the first atomic bomb had set the air on fire? Its builders had to check.
In 1942, Edward Teller asked: could the fireball get hot enough to fuse the nitrogen in the air, and spread?
Hans Bethe worked it by hand. The bomb would reach a few million degrees. Nitrogen nuclei need far more than that to fuse.
And air is thin. X-rays carry heat out of the fireball faster than fusion can add it. The flame starves in a fraction of a second.
A 1946 Los Alamos report checked again. Same answer. On July 16, 1945, Trinity lit the desert. The sky stayed.
In 1961, a bomb over 2,000 times bigger went off. Nothing. Bethe later wrote: it is not a matter of probabilities, it is simply impossible.

description:
What if the first atomic bomb had ignited the atmosphere? In 1942 Edward Teller raised exactly that worry, and Hans Bethe calculated the answer by hand.
A fission bomb heats air to a few million degrees, far short of what nitrogen nuclei need to fuse, and the thin air radiates heat away as X-rays faster than fusion could add it. A 1946 Los Alamos report confirmed the margin, the Trinity test went ahead on July 16, 1945, and the 50-megaton Tsar Bomba of 1961 came nowhere near igniting anything. Bethe wrote in 1975 that ignition is not a matter of probabilities but simply impossible.
What should we run through next?

first_comment: The famous 'three in a million' odds came from a 1959 interview, years after the test; Bethe said no such number was ever calculated. Which near-miss in science should we run through next?
